questions.stem: State what power means in terms of work done.
questions.modelAnswer: Power is the work done per unit time — equivalently, the rate of doing work or of transferring energy.

questions.stem: State what a power rating on an appliance shows.
questions.modelAnswer: The rating shows the amount of energy the appliance transfers per unit time, measured in watts.

questions.stem: Explain why two cars that do the same work can still be described as having different powers.
questions.modelAnswer: Power depends on time as well as on the amount of energy transferred. If both cars do the same work but one completes the transfer sooner, its energy-per-second rate is higher, so that car is the more powerful even though the total transfer is identical.

questions.stem: A train of power 1 MW runs for 20 s at full output. Calculate the energy it transfers.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy transferred = power × time = 1 000 000 × 20 = 20 000 000 J, so the train transfers 20 MJ in 20 seconds.

questions.stem: State the power equation in symbols and name each quantity with its unit.
questions.modelAnswer: P = W ÷ t, where P is power in watts, W is the work done in joules and t is the time taken in seconds.

questions.stem: State the unit of power and express one kilowatt in watts.
questions.modelAnswer: Power is measured in watts, and one kilowatt equals 1000 watts.

questions.stem: Explain why the time must be converted into seconds before using P = W ÷ t.
questions.modelAnswer: The watt is defined as one joule transferred per second, so the equation only produces watts when the time enters in seconds. Substituting minutes overstates the time by sixty, and the computed power falls by the same factor.

questions.stem: An electric oven of power 10 kW runs for 2 minutes. Calculate the energy it transfers.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert first: 10 kW = 10 000 W and 2 minutes = 120 s. Energy transferred = P × t = 10 000 × 120 = 1 200 000 J, so the oven transfers 1.2 MJ.
